I think this is an underratedly common experience. What makes it such a whiplash is that you're probably both at the beginning of a rather steep learning curve, but only just realizing that learning curve even exists. And reluctant to consider the implications, because of the impact it would have on your existing world model.

For inexperienced engineers it's that "your job is figuring shit out, not typing the code in", which for some people is like telling them that their dream job doesn't exist/the mental model most of their peers operate under isn't true.

For a manager it's that you can't really assume that everybody has the same personality/relationship to work/experience as you do, and that you might have even forgotten what it was like to be in their position, or not noticed how different some of your colleagues were from you. Which is also like telling them, "it turns out the best manager for your team is not the one you would want for yourself, and this job is going to be very different from what you thought".

I think it's very important to have a large enough sample of non-reporting colleagues across the range of experience. It helps you passively form a model of what normal career and even just life development looks like, and when you're in situations like this where you're not sure whether you're the asshole, or the other person is, or just confused, you can kind of in retrospect see how the near-peer may have navigated the same thing.

Same goes for interacting with enough non-developers and business people/customers/higherups to get some about the purpose of your role. Your role is downstream of what you do for them.

Architects are a bad meme, along the same lines as scrum masters and product managers. Good software engineers spend more time on design than implementation, and the best are helping their teammates with design, and auditing designs of adjacent teams to ensure integration success. So architecture is an important part of the job, but that doesn't mean that you can automatically declare a role with the title "architect" and make the whole organization better at design.

Architect roles are a bad meme because the architect always ends up knowing less about the system and how it is used than the engineers and support staff, yet they have more influence over the decisions affecting those things. That's the essence of an organizational anti-pattern/bad-meme any time it shows up: influence over resources anti-correlated with decision quality. Additionally, architects often report to non-technical folks fairly high up the chain. Those people are bad at screening for such a technical role, sometimes even making the mistake of replacing an architect with an external hire.

jameshart · Nov 21, 2026

All software development is architecture. Decide to implement a change by adding an if block to some code, by adding a function, by creating a new module and implementing it there, locally in the browser or on the server… those are all architectural decisions.

Large scale software development is just a nested series of architectural choices from top to bottom.

That some organizations choose to give some software developers the job title of architect is not a ‘bad meme’, it’s a reaction to the realization that there’s a lot of architectural decisions being made and it might be nice if all the people making them had sufficient information to make them right.

Good ‘architects’ focus on making sure developers who are making all those architectural decisions have the right context to make them.

Bad ‘architects’ try to make - or preempt, or second guess - all those decisions that have to be made. That doesn’t scale and doesn’t work.

I didn't understand this framing where a person is either a coder OR an architect, but not both, until I ran into a company that operated this way.

All of my jobs expected software developers to make and own their decisions, as well as ship at least some code related to the decisions they made.

The first time I encountered the coder-OR-architect separation was at a company that hired way too many people and held way too many meetings. They separated every responsibility out into different roles and then assigned those to different hires. There were so many roles that they couldn't even correctly identify the right boundaries between, for example, the Product Manager and the Product Designer, or the Project Manager and the Program Manager and the Engineering Manager.

The most surprising thing was how many people at that company liked it that way. The product managers liked writing up PRDs and then making them someone else's problems. The architects would translate those into big documents, then it was someone else's problem. The project managers would do elaborate ceremonies to turn them into tickets which became the coder's problem. The coders took the tickets and wrote enough code to close the ticket, then it became someone else's problem. Eventually the end product became the customer's problem.

I could see how comforting it was. You could settle into a constrained role and, as long you dutifully produced the artifacts of that role, it then left your plate and became someone else's problem. No one person held enough of the responsibility to be accountable for anything, because you could always point up and down the decision pipeline at someone else.

I think these people actually love AI, because it's yet another tool to defer work and responsibility to. They're the people who now point to Claude when something breaks, saying they'll get right on to having Claude fix it. It's one more step in the handoff pipeline and separation of accountability.
